<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, Ghauri is clearly an advanced, cross-platform command-line tool designed to automate the detection and exploitation of SQL injection vulnerabilities. It’s built in Python and organized modularly, which means we can break the system down into several logical components. Here’s a detailed explanation for drawing an accurate system design diagram tailored to this project:

1. Identify the Project Type and Purpose:
   • This is a security tool focused on SQL injection detection and exploitation.
   • Its primary role is to automate testing against various DBMS backends (e.g., MySQL, MSSQL, Postgres, Oracle) by sending crafted HTTP requests and analyzing responses.
   • The README lists a wide range of features and injection techniques, clearly showing it’s a feature-rich command-line security application.

2. Analyze the File Structure and Extract Main Architectural Components:
   • The project is organized within a “ghauri” directory that houses multiple sub-modules:
     - “common” module: Contains utilities (banner, colors, config, lib, payloads, pretty table formatting, session management, and miscellaneous utilities). This module supports the presentation and shared functionality across the tool.
     - “core” module: Encompasses primary functions like extraction, injection, sending requests, testing, and updating. This drives the core exploitation logic.
     - “dbms” module: Focused on fingerprinting the target database management systems to determine specifics (e.g., probably based on response signatures).
     - “extractor” module: Likely contains more advanced or specialized routines for payload extraction and additional intelligence gathering (both “advance.py” and “common.py”).
     - “logger” module: Implements a colored logger that prepares human-friendly output, ensuring that errors/info are easily distinguishable.
     - “scripts” module: Contains a command-line interface (CLI) script which acts as an entry point for the end user.
   • There are also configuration files like setup.py and requirements.txt which signal that the project is built as a Python package.

3. Architectural Relationships and Data Flow:
   • The entry point (likely the “ghauri/ghauri.py” or “scripts/ghauri.py”) accepts command-line parameters and parses the user’s input.
   • User input then flows into the core processing functions – the “core” module which orchestrates:
       - Preparation of HTTP requests (using the “core/request.py”).
       - Payload injection (via “core/inject.py”).
       - Extraction of data from the response (handled in “core/extract.py” and further supplemented by the “extractor” module).
   • The “common” directory provides support functions (configuration, utility functions, payload definitions, table formatting for output, session handling for storing state, etc.), which are used by almost every other module.
   • The “dbms” module takes the parsed HTTP responses, analyzes them for DBMS-specific indicators and fingerprints the possible back-end system.
   • Logging (via “logger/colored_logger.py”) records all events for debugging/info purposes.
   • The flow is iterative: the tool may resume, flush sessions, or update its execution strategies based on feedback from previous requests. There’s also support for updating itself through a built-in update mechanism (in “core/update.py”).

4. Design Guidelines for the Diagram:
   a. Main Components:
      • CLI / Script layer (Entry point)
      • Core Engine (with separate functions/modules for injection, extraction, and update routines)
      • Common Utilities (payloads, configurations, utilities, pretty printing, and session handling)
      • DBMS and Fingerprinting Module
      • Advanced Extraction Module
      • Logger Module for output management
   b. Relationships and Data Flow:
      • Draw directional arrows starting at the CLI input leading into the core engine.
      • Show the core engine interfacing with “common” utilities for configuration, payload management, and utility functions.
      • Connect the core engine to the “dbms” module for fingerprinting decisions and then to the requester that handles HTTP interactions.
      • Display the extraction pipeline where responses are parsed and results are processed, then sent to the logger and CLI for display.
      • Optionally, include arrows indicating invocation of “update” and “session” management as auxiliary processes.
   c. Architectural Patterns and Design Principles:
      • Highlight modularity: Each directory (common, core, extractor, dbms, logger, scripts) should be represented as an individual block/module.
      • Emphasize separation of concerns: input parsing (CLI) is separate from business logic (core module), which in turn isolates HTTP handling and payload extraction.
      • Note that the design is procedural and functionally modular – this isn’t a typical MVC web-app but a layered command-line utility structure.
   d. Technologies/Frameworks:
      • Python 3 is the primary language.
      • External libraries such as “prettytable” and possibly others for colored output are integrated into the common utilities.
      • The project uses pip for dependency management (requirements.txt) and setup.py for installation.

5. Tailoring the Diagram to a Full-Fledged Security Tool:
   • Since this isn’t a full-stack web application, instead of showing a frontend-backend separation, focus the emphasis on data flow from the CLI entry through the injection and extraction pipelines.
   • Make sure to show how HTTP request crafting, payload injection, and result extraction are interrelated.
   • Demonstrate the iterative flow when exploiting a target and integrating different injection techniques.

6. Instructing the Principal Software Engineer on Diagram Elements:
   • Ensure that each module/block is clearly labeled (e.g., “CLI Interface”, “Core Injection Logic”, “Payload & Config Utilities”, “DBMS Fingerprinting”, “Advanced Extraction”, “Logging”).
   • Use directional arrows to depict:
         – Data flow: e.g., from CLI → Core Injection → HTTP Request Handler → DBMS Fingerprinting, and then from response back to Extraction and Logger.
         – Dependencies: e.g., Core modules depend on common utilities.
   • Incorporate color coding or distinct shapes to distinguish between:
         – User-facing components (CLI, Logger)
         – Core functional components (Injection, Extraction, DBMS handling)
         – Support utilities (Common, Configuration, Payloads)
   • Annotate the diagram where needed with key configuration switches (like update, session flush, proxy usage) showing optional flows.

By following these guidelines, you should produce a detailed system design diagram that accurately represents Ghauri’s modular architecture and the interactions between its major components. Use your favorite diagramming tool to sketch out these elements, ensuring clarity and the inclusion of all essential modules and data flows.
</explanation>
